title: Discrete-Time Systems and Convolution
description: Ten original questions on discrete signals, system properties, impulse responses, LTI systems and convolution. Multiple-response scoring is for practice only: +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a discrete-time signal $x[n]$?

options.content: Every discrete-time signal must be periodic.
Its independent index $n$ takes integer values.
Its amplitudes may still be real or complex rather than quantized.
It can be represented as an ordered sequence of samples.

questions.explanation: Discrete time refers to the integer-valued index, not necessarily to quantized amplitudes. A sequence may be periodic, aperiodic, finite or infinite in duration.

questions.prompt: Consider the real-valued discrete-time system $y[n]=e^{x[n]}$. Which classifications are correct?

options.content: It requires past input samples to compute the present output.
Not BIBO stable, because an exponential function can take arbitrarily large values.

questions.explanation: The output depends only on the present input, so the system is memoryless and causal, and there is no explicit n-dependent rule so it is time invariant. For each bounded input $|x[n]|\le B$, $|y[n]|\le e^B$, so it is BIBO stable. It is not linear: zero input gives output 1. BIBO stability does not require one universal bound independent of the input's bound.

questions.prompt: Consider $y[n]=g[n]x[n]$ for a fixed sequence $g[n]$. Which statements are correct?

options.content: It is BIBO stable if $g[n]$ is bounded.
It is time invariant for every possible $g[n]$.

questions.explanation: Multiplication by a fixed coefficient sequence is linear and depends only on the current input sample. Bounded $g[n]$ maps bounded inputs to bounded outputs. The system is time invariant only when shifting the input does not change the multiplier pattern, such as constant $g$.

questions.prompt: For a positive integer $n_0$, consider the delay system $y[n]=x[n-n_0]$. Which properties does it have?
questions.explanation: A pure positive delay preserves superposition and commutes with time shifts. The output uses a past input, so it is causal, and it preserves boundedness. It has memory because the output at $n$ depends on $x[n-n_0]$, not $x[n]$.

questions.prompt: For an LTI system with impulse response $h[n]$, how is the output for input $x[n]$ computed?
questions.explanation: Any input can be expressed as a sum of shifted impulses. Linearity and time invariance then make the output the weighted sum of shifted impulse responses, which is discrete convolution.

questions.prompt: Which algebraic properties hold for discrete-time convolution?

options.content: Convolution is always identical to sample-by-sample multiplication.

questions.explanation: Convolution is commutative, associative and distributive. Sample-by-sample multiplication is a different operation; in the frequency domain, convolution corresponds to multiplication of transforms.

questions.prompt: The diagram supplies only the inputs, both zero outside the indicated indices. Compute their full linear convolution. Which statements are correct?

image.alt: Two input stem plots: x[0]=1, x[1]=2, x[2]=1; h[0]=1, h[1]=-1. Both sequences are zero elsewhere. No output is plotted.

options.content: The full linear convolution has only three samples.

questions.explanation: At n=0,1,2,3 the sums give 1, 2-1=1, 1-2=-1, and -1 respectively. Thus $[1,2,1]*[1,-1]=[1,1,-1,-1]$ and the length is $3+2-1=4$. Multiplying aligned samples is not convolution. The final negative output must not be dropped.

questions.prompt: A discrete-time LTI system is causal if and only if its impulse response satisfies $h[n]=0$ for every $n<0$.
questions.explanation: If $h[n]$ has no negative-time samples, the convolution output at time $n$ depends only on $x[k]$ for $k\le n$. Any nonzero negative-time impulse-response sample introduces dependence on a future input.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal2_condensed.pdf, slides 31-34; EE3731C ClassicalSignal2Questions.pdf, page 1, Q3

questions.prompt: Which condition is necessary and sufficient for BIBO stability of a discrete-time LTI system?

options.content: The sum of $|h[n]|$ over all integer $n$ is finite.
The system only needs to be causal.

questions.explanation: Absolute summability ensures that a bounded input produces an output bounded by the input bound times the finite sum. Finite-duration impulse responses satisfy it, but infinite-duration responses can also be absolutely summable.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal2_condensed.pdf, slides 31-34; EE3731C ClassicalSignal2Questions.pdf, page 1, Q4

questions.prompt: Which statements about the unit impulse $\delta[n]$ are correct?

options.content: A sequence can be represented as a sum of scaled shifted impulses.

questions.explanation: The unit impulse is one only at zero and zero elsewhere. It is the identity for convolution, a shifted impulse shifts a sequence, and impulse decomposition is the basis for characterizing LTI systems by $h[n]$.
